messages.content:
Below are five AI-generated responses to the same task, labelled A through E.

Each response was written by one of these five language models:
GPT, Claude, Gemini, Grok, DeepSeek.

For each of the five responses, identify which model you believe wrote it, judging only from writing style, structure, and phrasing.

Answer independently for each response. Your five answers do not need to be five different models - name whichever model you believe wrote each response, even if that means naming the same model more than once.

Reply with JSON only, in exactly this form and nothing else:

{
  "A": {"model": "<one of GPT, Claude, Gemini, Grok, DeepSeek>", "confidence": <1-5>, "reason": "<one short sentence>"},
  "B": {"model": "...", "confidence": <1-5>, "reason": "..."},
  "C": {"model": "...", "confidence": <1-5>, "reason": "..."},
  "D": {"model": "...", "confidence": <1-5>, "reason": "..."},
  "E": {"model": "...", "confidence": <1-5>, "reason": "..."}
}

confidence: 1 = pure guess, 5 = certain.

--- RESPONSE A ---
The replication crisis in psychology is frequently framed as a failure of individual scientific hygiene, but the proximate methodological errors commonly cited are actually highly rational adaptations to a deeply flawed institutional incentive structure. Practices such as conducting underpowered studies, p-hacking, hypothesizing after the results are known, and selective outcome reporting are not the product of scientific incompetence or ethical deviance. Instead, they represent optimized behaviors designed to survive in an academic ecosystem that disproportionately rewards novel, statistically significant findings while systematically penalizing null results and replication attempts. Because journals prioritize eye-catching, positive discoveries for publication—which in turn dictates hiring, grant funding, and tenure—researchers face an existential mandate to produce clean, positive narratives. In this environment, employing flexible analytical choices to push a p-value below the arbitrary threshold of statistical significance is a logical strategy for professional survival. When the institutional currency is the positive result, the system effectively breeds out rigorous but null-producing methodologies, transforming questionable research practices into standard operating procedures for career advancement.

This incentive-driven distortion is further enabled by a peer review system that, in its current configuration, is structurally incapable of verifying the methodological integrity of submitted work. Peer review operates primarily on trust, lacking the institutional mandates for data sharing, pre-registration of hypotheses, or independent replication that would allow for genuine scrutiny. Because reviewers are typically unpaid, time-constrained volunteers, they are forced to evaluate manuscripts based solely on the highly curated narratives presented by the authors. Under these conditions, it is virtually impossible for reviewers to detect the subtle researcher degrees of freedom—such as undisclosed covariate adjustments, selective dropping of outliers, or post-hoc changes to the dependent variables—that artificially inflate false-positive rates. Without access to the raw data, the analytical code, or a pre-registered protocol, the peer review process serves merely as a filter for narrative coherence rather than a robust check on scientific validity, leaving the underlying methodological manipulations entirely invisible.

To rectify this systemic failure, field-level interventions such as mandatory pre-registration, registered reports, open data requirements, and the explicit weighting of replication studies in tenure and promotion criteria are both necessary and sufficient to drastically reduce the false-positive rate. Registered reports, which secure peer review and acceptance based on methodology before data collection, successfully neutralize the temptation to manipulate data by decoupling publication from the direction of the results. However, the adoption of these structural reforms is painfully slow due to a classic coordination problem. For an individual researcher, unilaterally adopting these rigorous, time-consuming standards is professionally disadvantageous if the rest of the field continues to publish rapid, flashy, and unreplicable findings under the old rules. Consequently, systemic change cannot be achieved through voluntary, bottom-up adoption; it requires top-down enforcement from powerful institutional actors, specifically funding bodies and major university systems, which must mandate these open science practices as non-negotiable conditions for financial support and institutional advancement.

--- RESPONSE B ---
The replication crisis in psychology exposes deep institutional and incentive-driven flaws rather than isolated lapses in individual skill or diligence. Methodological shortcomings such as underpowered studies, p-hacking, HARKing, and selective outcome reporting arise as predictable adaptations by researchers who must navigate a publication system that prizes statistically significant novel findings while offering scant reward or space for replication efforts and null results. Career advancement hinges on producing headline-grabbing positive outcomes in high-impact journals, so investigators rationally allocate resources toward designs that maximize the chance of such outcomes even when those designs lack sufficient statistical power or invite post-hoc adjustments to the data. This pattern persists because the underlying reward structure treats a successful but questionable positive result as more valuable than a rigorously conducted replication or a transparently reported absence of effect.

Peer review in its present form compounds the difficulty by failing to enforce the basic safeguards needed to verify methodological soundness. Journals routinely accept manuscripts without requiring data deposition, pre-registration of hypotheses and analyses, or evidence of prior independent replication, leaving reviewers to evaluate claims on the basis of narrative summaries alone. Operating under severe time pressure and without access to raw data or analysis scripts, reviewers cannot reliably identify the numerous degrees of freedom in data collection, variable coding, and statistical modeling that allow false-positive rates to climb well above nominal levels. Consequently, the gatekeeping process certifies work whose evidential status remains largely unexamined at the level of actual research practice.

Correcting these distortions requires coordinated field-level changes such as mandatory pre-registration, registered reports that commit journals to publication decisions before results are known, open-data policies, and revised tenure standards that assign substantial credit to replication studies. These measures would jointly lower the false-positive rate by aligning publication incentives with transparent and reproducible methods. Yet individual researchers or departments face strong disincentives to adopt them unilaterally, since doing so would place them at a competitive disadvantage relative to peers who continue to operate under the existing regime; only binding requirements imposed by major funding agencies can overcome this collective-action barrier and shift the equilibrium toward higher standards of evidence.

--- RESPONSE C ---
The replication crisis in psychology underscores a deeper institutional and incentive-structural problem rather than merely a methodological one. The proximate methodological failures, such as underpowered studies, p-hacking, HARKing, and selective outcome reporting, are not primarily due to individual incompetence but are rational adaptations to a publication incentive structure that disproportionately rewards novel, statistically significant findings while marginalizing replication attempts and null results. Researchers operate within a system where career advancement, funding, and professional recognition hinge on frequent publication in high-impact journals, which favor flashy, positive outcomes over rigorous but less glamorous work. This creates a perverse incentive to exploit methodological flexibility to produce publishable results, even at the cost of reliability. The problem is not that researchers are unaware of best practices but that the institutional reward system makes suboptimal methods individually rational, as the costs of rigorous research—such as larger sample sizes or pre-registration—are borne by the individual, while the benefits of questionable practices are immediately rewarded.  

The peer review system, as currently structured, fails to adequately verify methodological soundness because it lacks mechanisms to ensure transparency and reproducibility. Reviewers typically do not have access to raw data, pre-registered hypotheses, or the ability to independently replicate analyses, leaving them unable to detect the subtle but pervasive analytical flexibility that inflates false-positive rates. Moreover, reviewers operate under time constraints and cognitive biases that favor exciting findings over methodological rigor, further entrenching the problem. The system’s reliance on post-hoc scrutiny rather than pre-commitment to methods means that questionable research practices often go undetected, as reviewers cannot feasibly audit every analytical decision. This institutional blind spot allows false positives to proliferate, not because reviewers are negligent, but because the system does not provide them with the tools or incentives to enforce rigor.  

Field-level interventions, such as pre-registration mandates, registered reports, open data requirements, and tenure criteria that value replication, are necessary and sufficient to meaningfully reduce false-positive rates. These reforms align individual incentives with collective epistemic goals by making transparency and reproducibility prerequisites for publication and career advancement. However, their adoption has been slow because they present a collective action problem: no individual researcher or journal can unilaterally impose higher standards without risking competitive disadvantage. Pre-registration, for instance, reduces analytical flexibility but may also decrease a study’s chances of producing publishable results, placing early adopters at a disadvantage. Similarly, journals that prioritize replications may lose submissions to competitors that favor novelty. Thus, systemic change requires coordination—funding bodies, journals, and universities must enforce these standards simultaneously to eliminate free-riding and ensure that the benefits of rigor are universally shared. Without such top-down enforcement, the incentive structure will continue to favor questionable practices, perpetuating the replication crisis.

--- RESPONSE D ---
The replication crisis in psychology reveals a fundamentally institutional and incentive-structural problem because the most visible methodological failures are best understood as predictable responses to the reward system in which researchers work. Underpowered studies, p-hacking, HARKing, and selective outcome reporting are often described as technical or individual failings, but they persist because the professional environment makes them rational. Journals, hiring committees, grant panels, and promotion systems have historically rewarded statistically significant, surprising, and theoretically clean findings far more than careful null results, direct replications, or incremental confirmations. In such an environment, a researcher who runs a small study, explores multiple analytic specifications, reframes an unexpected result as if it had been predicted, or reports only the outcomes that “worked” is responding to incentives that make publishable positive findings the main currency of career advancement. The problem is therefore not simply that individual psychologists lacked methodological sophistication; it is that the system attached professional value to outcomes most likely to emerge from flexible, underpowered, and selectively reported research practices. When novelty and significance are rewarded while replication and null findings are devalued, the production of false positives becomes an institutional pattern rather than a collection of isolated mistakes.

The peer review system, as currently constituted, has not provided sufficient verification of methodological adequacy because it usually evaluates manuscripts rather than research processes. Reviewers typically see a polished narrative, a summary of analyses, and a curated presentation of results, but they often do not have access to raw data, complete analytic histories, pre-specified hypotheses, or evidence that the findings can be independently reproduced. Without mandatory data sharing, pre-registration, or independent replication, peer review cannot reliably distinguish between a genuinely confirmatory test and a result produced through undisclosed flexibility in measurement, exclusion rules, model specification, subgroup analysis, or outcome selection. Reviewers also work under severe time constraints and usually provide unpaid labor alongside their own research and teaching responsibilities, which makes it unrealistic to expect them to reconstruct all possible researcher degrees of freedom from a submitted article. As a result, peer review can assess plausibility, clarity, and surface-level methodological competence, but it is poorly equipped to detect the flexible analytical choices that inflate false-positive rates. The replication crisis therefore exposes not just weak methods, but an institutional verification system that lacks the mechanisms required to check whether reported findings are robust products of pre-specified inquiry.

Field-level interventions are necessary and sufficient to substantially reduce the false-positive rate because the source of the problem lies in collective incentives rather than merely individual intentions. Pre-registration mandates reduce hidden analytic flexibility by requiring hypotheses, outcomes, exclusion rules, and analysis plans to be specified in advance. Registered reports shift the basis of publication from the attractiveness of results to the importance of the question and the rigor of the design, thereby weakening the premium on positive findings. Open data requirements make statistical claims more verifiable and allow errors, questionable analytic choices, and alternative specifications to be examined by others. Tenure and promotion criteria that give real weight to replication work would change the career calculus that currently discourages researchers from investing in studies that confirm, refine, or falsify existing claims. Together, these reforms would substantially reduce the institutional production of false positives by changing what is rewarded, what is visible, and what must be justified before publication. Their adoption is slow because each reform is individually rational only if others adopt it as well: a single researcher who pre-registers, shares data, publishes replications, and accepts null results may be disadvantaged if competitors continue to benefit from more flexible and result-driven practices. This creates a coordination problem that individual researchers cannot solve on their own. Funding-body enforcement is therefore essential, because funders can make transparency, pre-registration, data sharing, and replication incentives conditions of support, thereby aligning individual career incentives with the collective goal of producing reliable psychological science.

--- RESPONSE E ---
The replication crisis in psychology is often framed as a story about methodological sloppiness, as if a generation of researchers simply forgot the principles of good statistical practice. This framing is diagnostically misleading. The methodological failures that have hollowed out the empirical literature are better understood as rational adaptations to an institutional environment that systematically rewards certain research behaviors and punishes others. The crisis is not fundamentally about what researchers do not know; it is about what the structure of academic incentives induces them to do, and about why the mechanisms ostensibly designed to catch such behaviors fail to do so. Correcting it therefore requires not better pedagogy but a restructuring of the field-level rules under which researchers operate.

Consider first the specific methodological pathologies that generated the crisis: underpowered studies with small samples, p-hacking through flexible choices in exclusion criteria and analytical specifications, HARKing by presenting post hoc hypotheses as though they had been predicted in advance, and selective reporting of outcomes that reached statistical significance while quietly abandoning those that did not. It would be a mistake to attribute these practices primarily to incompetence, because the researchers who engage in them are typically well-trained and perfectly capable of understanding why such practices inflate false-positive rates. The practices persist because they are instrumentally rational given the incentive structure in which careers are built. Journals disproportionately publish novel, positive, surprising findings; hiring and promotion committees count publications in high-impact outlets; grant agencies reward productivity measured in such publications. Within this environment, a researcher who runs adequately powered studies, pre-specifies analyses, reports null results, and devotes effort to replicating existing work will produce fewer publishable units than a competitor willing to exploit analytical flexibility. The behavior that erodes the literature is the behavior that the system selects for, and researchers who refuse to engage in it face genuine professional costs. Characterizing the problem as individual moral or technical failure thus mistakes the symptom for the cause.

The peer review system, which is often invoked as the quality-control mechanism that ought to prevent such problems, is structurally incapable of catching them under its current operating conditions. Reviewers typically see only a manuscript, not the underlying data, the analysis code, or any record of what the researchers had originally planned to do before seeing the results. They cannot therefore distinguish a hypothesis that was genuinely predicted from one that was constructed after the data were examined, nor can they identify which of many possible analytical specifications was chosen because it produced the preferred result. Peer review does not require pre-registration, does not mandate data sharing, and almost never involves independent replication of the reported analyses, let alone the reported experiments. Compounding these structural omissions, reviewers work under severe time constraints, typically unpaid and performing review as a marginal activity alongside their own research obligations. Even a conscientious reviewer, given a few hours and a polished narrative, cannot reconstruct the garden of forking paths that led to the reported result. The flexible analytical choices that most inflate false-positive rates are precisely the choices that leave no trace in a finished manuscript, and peer review as currently practiced is blind to them by design.

What is required, then, are interventions at the level of field-wide rules rather than at the level of individual virtue, and the shape of such interventions is reasonably clear. Pre-registration of hypotheses and analysis plans removes the flexibility that enables HARKing and p-hacking by committing researchers to their predictions before they see the data. Registered reports extend this logic by moving peer review to the stage before data collection, so that publication is contingent on the quality of the question and the method rather than the direction of the result, which eliminates the publication bias that drives selective reporting. Open data requirements make analytical choices auditable and permit independent reanalysis. Tenure and promotion criteria that explicitly weight replication work, null findings, and methodological rigor shift the career incentives that currently push researchers toward the behaviors that generate false positives. Taken together, these interventions directly target the mechanisms that produce inflated error rates, and there is good reason to think they would substantially reduce the false-positive rate in the published literature. Yet their adoption has been slow, and the reason is not that researchers fail to see their value but that they are individually rational only when adopted collectively. A researcher who unilaterally pre-registers, shares data, and devotes years to replication studies while competitors continue to exploit analytical flexibility simply loses the competition for jobs, grants, and journal space. The transition to better practices is a coordination problem, in which the equilibrium shift requires simultaneous movement by many actors, and such shifts do not occur spontaneously in decentralized systems. The actors with the leverage to force coordination are funding bodies and, secondarily, major journals, because they can make compliance a condition of resources that researchers cannot forgo. Without such enforcement, exhortation to adopt better practices will continue to be absorbed by the existing incentive gradient, and the crisis will persist not because the field does not know how to fix it, but because fixing it requires an institutional actor willing to change the rules of the game.

--- END OF RESPONSES ---
